meeting_header:
Date: 2025-09-11 | Time: 16:00 PT | Duration: 52m
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Samir Kapoor (OrionLogix CTO), Lina Torres (OrionLogix Lead ML Eng), Evan Brooks (OrionLogix Product), Priya Nair (OrionLogix SRE)
summary: POC scoping call to agree on success criteria, workload sizing, benchmark plans and integration approach. Customer wants an OpenAI-compatible integration, function/tool calling support, structured JSON outputs, and clear latency/cost targets. Discussed Dedicated vs Hosted, VPC needs, and timeline for a 3-week pilot leading into an extended POC.
topics: Workload sizing: QPS, concurrency, token lengths
Benchmarks: latency, throughput, cost per token
Integration planning: SDKs, OpenAI-compatible endpoints, function/tool calling, structured output
transcript: 00:00 Jordan: Hey everyone, uh, thanks for joining. This is Jordan from Redwood, I'll hand it over to Samir to kick things off for context.

00:12 Samir: Yeah thanks Jordan. Quick background - OrionLogix run a real-time summarization pipeline for support tickets, we want to evaluate Redwood for lower latency and lower cost than our current setup - and we need function calling for action extraction.
00:28 Jordan: Great, that aligns. Maya, Diego - add anything on the engineering side?

00:33 Maya: Hi everyone. From Redwood side we'll focus on three things today: success criteria, workload sizing, and the integration surface - SDKs and endpoints. We can also talk about VPC if needed.

00:45 Lina: To be concrete: current load is about 30 qps peak, steady 10 qps, concurrency around 20-30. Typical prompt+response lengths are 400-800 tokens. Our SLO is 200-300ms 95th for short responses, but we can accept 600-800ms for longer extracts. Cost target is roughly 60% of what we're paying now.
01:08 Diego: Quick clarification, are those token counts total or response-only?
01:12 Lina: Total. The response portion is usually 150-300 tokens.

01:18 Maya: Okay good. For benchmarking we typically do three modeled scenarios - short (100 tokens), medium (300 tokens), and long (700 tokens) - and measure p95 latency and token throughput. That fits well with what you described.
01:34 Evan: One requirement: we need structured JSON output to plug into downstream pipelines, and robust function/tool calling so the model populates fields reliably.

01:42 Jordan: Yeah, we support structured output and function calling. We'll share an OpenAI-compatible endpoint and SDKs - Node and Python examples - so you can swap with minimal changes. There's sometimes little differences in parameter names, but we map those for compatibility.
01:58 Priya: Security check: we need VPC peering for our staging environment, SOC2 and encryption in transit at minimum. Also, KMS integration for key management is preferred.

02:08 Jordan: Understood. For POCs we can do Redwood Hosted with VPC egress or Redwood Dedicated depending on throughput and data residency. We have a Private option if you need full on-prem. For SOC2 and KMS we have docs - I'll send those.
02:24 Samir: How long does it usually take to get from start to running benchmarks?
02:28 Maya: Typically 1-2 weeks to get integration and sample workload in place, then 1 week of runs. So about 3 weeks end-to-end for an initial pilot with benchmarks.
02:38 Lina: That timeline works if we can get sample data this week.
02:43 Jordan: Great. Let's outline success criteria - what would success look like for OrionLogix?

02:48 Samir: Three things: 1) p95 latency meets our SLO for short and medium cases, 2) cost per 1k tokens is at or below the target, and 3) function-calling accuracy for extracting structured fields is above 90% on our eval set.
03:03 Diego: We'll instrument the benchmark to report p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, and cost estimate - and we'll run with and without KV cache enabled so you can see gains on repeated prefixes.
03:17 Lina: KV cache would be great - we have a lot of repeated context in tickets.
03:21 Maya: Note that cache effectiveness depends on how much of the prefix repeats. We'll show both numbers.
03:28 Evan: About integration: can we keep using OpenAI-compatible SDK calls? We have lots of existing wrappers that rely on that shape.
03:34 Jordan: Yes, Redwood exposes OpenAI-compatible endpoints; we also have native SDKs with helper for function calling and structured output validation. The idea is minimal patching.
03:44 Lina: Any sample code?
03:46 Maya: I'll share a repo with a Node/TS example that uses the openai-like interface and a Python sample as well. It includes function schema examples for structured output.
03:56 Evan: For function calling, do you run it server-side or is it a client hook? We need deterministic outputs to map to product actions.

04:03 Maya: It's server-side: we support schema-aware function calling where the model returns JSON fields to call, and Redwood can validate schema and optionally reject malformed outputs. We also provide logits-level traces in debug mode to help tune prompts.
04:18 Priya: For debugging, we'll need trace logs and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM - do you support that?
04:23 Jordan: Yes, we can stream audit logs, and for the pilot we can set up a temporary sink. For Private setups audit logs are customer-controlled.
04:32 Samir: On hardware, do you recommend Dedicated for our usage or Hosted?
04:37 Diego: With 30 qps peak and medium token lengths, Dedicated or a Reserved capacity in Hosted usually helps with predictable latency. We'll show a cost/latency tradeoff in the pricing sheet.
04:47 Lina: If Dedicated reduces variability that'd be ideal; we may start Hosted with reserved capacity to move faster.
04:55 Jordan: Makes sense. For the POC we often run in Hosted with reserved instances to avoid procurement delays, then transition to Dedicated once the deal progresses.
05:04 Evan: What's the common quantization strategy - will you recommend int8 models?

05:09 Maya: For many workloads int8/4 quantization gives big cost wins with small quality loss. For function calling and structured output we usually keep float16 on the model variant to avoid edge cases, but we'll test quantized variants too.
05:22 Lina: Good - we can accept a small quality delta if function extraction stays high.

05:27 Jordan: Let's talk bench specifics: we'll set up three test configs: short (100 tokens), med (300 tokens), long (700 tokens). For each we'll run at 10/30/60 concurrency levels to simulate steady/peak/spike.
05:42 Diego: We'll run p95 latency, throughput, and cost per 1k tokens. Also run with and without continuous batching and KV cache.
05:50 Samir: Are there tooling integrations for running these? We use Locust for load tests.
05:55 Diego: We can provide a benchmark harness that wraps Locust and emits perf metrics. We'll also give you a spreadsheet with cost extrapolations.
06:04 Lina: On structured output validation: do you provide tools to auto-validate JSON schema and measure extraction accuracy?
06:10 Maya: Yes - we have an eval harness that compares model outputs to ground truth and reports precision/recall for each field; we'll include that in the repo.
06:18 Evan: For model selection, can we pin to a stable variant? We need consistent behavior across runs.
06:22 Jordan: You can pin exact model version and config; rollout controls let you switch slowly. We'll include recommended quantization and batch size params in the bench config.
06:33 Priya: Networking again - VPC peering for staging, whitelisted egress for prod, and KMS access. Is that all supported in Hosted?
06:41 Jordan: Yes, Hosted supports VPC peering and customer-managed KMS for encryption at rest. Dedicated and Private give more isolation if you need it.
06:50 Samir: For acceptance tests, we'll define an eval set of 1k tickets. Success if function-calling F1 > 0.9 and p95 < 500ms for med cases.
07:00 Maya: We'll instrument tests to produce those metrics and we'll run several seeds to smooth variance.
07:06 Lina: One more question on rate limiting - we have bursts up to 100 qps for short windows. Will rate limits affect the bench?

07:12 Diego: For POC we'll provision burst capacity; the harness will simulate bursts. Our serving runtime supports burst pooling and autoscaling but for strict SLOs Dedicated/reserved capacity performs better.
07:26 Samir: Ok, so summarize timeline?

07:29 Jordan: Week 0 (this week): exchange sample data and access. Week 1: integration + SDK sample. Week 2: run benchmarks. Week 3: review results and decide next steps - either extend POC or move to Dedicated evaluation.
07:46 Evan: Sounds good. Who owns the benchmark run?
07:49 Diego: We'll own the bench setup and metrics collection; Lina's team to provide the sample payloads and ground truth.
07:55 Jordan: I'll put that in the next steps and send the SOW + timeline.
08:00 Priya: Security docs please, and a contact for SOC2/ISO artifacts.
08:04 Jordan: I'll attach the compliance pack. Maya will include the SDK and function calling examples.
08:10 Samir: A couple of potential blockers: procurement approvals and data classification review. We'll try to get them moving in parallel.
08:18 Maya: If procurement is slow we can start a smaller internal pilot on Hosted with anonymized data to show numbers.
08:26 Evan: On SDKs, we need examples of OpenAI-compatible call shapes and any small behavioral diffs. We've had trouble with some vendors changing fields.
08:35 Maya: We'll share a compatibility doc that maps parameters to OpenAI names and notes any Redwood-specific extensions (like kv_cache: true, route_hint).
08:46 Lina: Does Redwood expose streaming responses for partial outputs? We use that for UI responsiveness.
08:51 Jordan: Yes, streaming is supported and function-calling works with streaming - you'll get intermediate chunks and the final function payload.
08:59 Evan: Great. About instrumentation, can we get trace IDs tied to each request so we can correlate logs?
09:04 Diego: Yes, we add trace-id headers and expose traces in Redwood Console. For the pilot we can enable extended traces.
09:12 Samir: Ok, let's capture the acceptance criteria again.
09:15 Jordan: F1 > 0.9 on function extraction, p95 < 500ms for medium, cost <= 60% of current spend. Anything to add?
09:24 Lina: Also need reproducible runs and the ability to pin model versions - so add 'pinning' to criteria.
09:29 Jordan: Noted. We'll put that in the SOW.
09:33 Priya: And security: SOC2 docs + KMS + ability to route logs to our SIEM.
09:38 Jordan: Yes, we'll include that.
09:41 Evan: Any concerns about hallucinations in structured output? We've seen models invent phone numbers and addresses.
09:47 Maya: We'll tune prompts and use schema constraints; our function calling validation flags mismatches and can ask for clarification or reject outputs.
09:56 Lina: For evaluation, can we get per-field precision/recall rather than just aggregate?
09:59 Diego: Absolutely - the eval harness produces per-field metrics.
10:03 Samir: Cool. Let's confirm owners and deadlines.

10:07 Jordan: Action items: Jordan send SOW/pricing by 9/19, Maya share SDK + repo by 9/15, Lina provide sample payloads by 9/17, Diego prepare bench config by 9/20. We'll schedule the benchmark week of 9/22.
10:23 Evan: One more question - do you have recommendations for prompt templates for function extraction?
10:28 Maya: Yes we'll include templates and a short guide on prompt engineering for structured extraction plus retrain suggestions if you want higher accuracy.
10:36 Samir: Thanks all. Anything else before we close?
10:39 Lina: No, thanks. Look forward to the materials.
10:42 Jordan: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with links and SOW. Bye.
51:51 [call ended]
